en: The *Treatise on the Shattering of Characteristics* by Master Bodhidharma states:
"If there is a person who aspires to seek the Buddha-way, what dharma should they practice that is most concise and essential? He replied:
"Only the single dharma of contemplating the mind (citta) comprehensively subsumes all dharmas; it is the most concise and essential. He asked: "What single dharma is able to..."
Regarding the subsumption of all phenomena, the answer is: The mind is the root of the myriad dharmas. All phenomena are produced solely by the mind.
If one can thoroughly understand the mind, then the myriad dharmas are fully present.

It is just as all branches, flowers, and fruits of a great tree depend entirely upon the root; one who plants a tree preserves the root to bring forth growth, while one who fells a tree removes the root.

One must die [to this delusion]. If one understands the mind and cultivates the Way, it will be accomplished with little effort and ease. If one cultivates without understanding the mind, labor will be wasted and there will be no benefit.
Therefore, know that all good and evil arise from one's own mind; to seek them elsewhere outside the mind is ultimately impossible.
Question: How does one observe the mind such that it is termed "thoroughly understood"? Answer:

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they thoroughly understand that the four great elements and the five aggregates are fundamentally empty and without self; they clearly perceive the arising and functioning of their own mind.
There are two kinds of distinctions. What are the two? First is the pure mind; second is the defiled mind. These two types of mental phenomena are also naturally and originally coexistent.

Although they depend upon the convergence of conditions and mutually rely on one another, the pure mind always delights in wholesome causes, while the defiled essence constantly contemplates evil karma. If one does not undergo such defilement, one is then called a sage. Thus...

One can distance oneself from all suffering and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa. However, if one falls into a defiled mind and creates karma, becoming shrouded by its entanglements, one is termed an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Such a person sinks into the three realms and undergoes various sufferings. Why is this? Because that defiled mind obstructs the essence of *tathatā* (suchness).
Thus, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Within the bodies of sentient beings, there exists the diamond-like Buddha-nature, which is like the sun."

The wheel is luminous in essence, perfect, vast, and boundless. Yet, it is shrouded by the heavy clouds of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), like the light of a lamp inside a jar that cannot manifest itself.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;

because it is covered by ignorance (*avidyā*), they do not attain liberation. Buddha-nature is precisely the nature of awakening (*bodhi*). It is simply the awakening to oneself and the awakening of others. Awakening...
To know with clear understanding is what is called liberation. Thus, one knows that all wholesome qualities have awakening as their root.
By means of this root of awakening, one is able to manifest the trees of merit and the fruit of the virtue of nirvāṇa; it is through this that they are accomplished.
To contemplate the mind in this way may be called "understanding."

Question: It was stated above that True Suchness (tathatā) and Buddha-nature take awakening as their root for all meritorious qualities. I do not yet understand what serves as the root for the mind of ignorance (avidyā). Answer: Although the mind of ignorance possesses eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. This is because the mind of awakening is the fundamental substance; the mind of ignorance is merely adventitious dust. Therefore, when one awakens to the mind of awakening, the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires are simultaneously extinguished. Thus, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. Furthermore, the mind of awakening is the root of all dharmas. Why? Because all dharmas arise from the mind. If the mind is pure, then all dharmas are pure. If the mind is defiled, then all dharmas are defiled. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. Moreover, the mind of awakening is the root of all Buddhas. Why? Because all Buddhas attain Buddhahood through this mind. If there were no such mind, there would be no Buddhas. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. Furthermore, the mind of awakening is the root of all sentient beings. Why? Because all sentient beings are born from this mind. If there were no such mind, there would be no sentient beings. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. Additionally, the mind of awakening is the root of all phenomena. Why? Because all phenomena are produced by this mind. If there were no such mind, there would be no phenomena. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. Finally, the mind of awakening is the root of the Dharma. Why? Because the Dharma arises from this mind. If there were no such mind, there would be no Dharma. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. For these reasons, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is like a great tree: although it has many branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, they all have the root as their basis. If the root is cut, then the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all perish. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great ocean: although it contains immeasurable waves, bubbles, and foam, they all have the water as their root. If the water dries up, then the waves, bubbles, and foam will all vanish. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great mirror: although it reflects immeasurable forms and images, they all have the mirror as their root. If the mirror is broken, then the forms and images will all disappear. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great fire: although it produces immeasurable smoke, flames, and sparks, they all have the fire as their root. If the fire is extinguished, then the smoke, flames, and sparks will all cease. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great wind: although it stirs immeasurable clouds, mist, and dust, they all have the wind as their root. If the wind ceases, then the clouds, mist, and dust will all settle. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great mountain: although it has immeasurable peaks, valleys, and caves, they all have the mountain as their root. If the mountain crumbles, then the peaks, valleys, and caves will all collapse. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great physician: although he prescribes immeasurable medicines and treatments, they all have the physician as their root. If the physician dies, then the medicines and treatments will all be ineffective. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great king: although he has immeasurable ministers, subjects, and retinues, they all have the king as their root. If the king is deposed, then the ministers, subjects, and retinues will all disperse. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great sun: although it emits immeasurable light and heat, they all have the sun as their root. If the sun sets, then the light and heat will all vanish. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great moon: although it displays immeasurable coolness and brightness, they all have the moon as their root. If the moon wanes, then the coolness and brightness will all fade. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great earth: although it supports immeasurable mountains, rivers, and forests, they all have the earth as their root. If the earth is destroyed, then the mountains, rivers, and forests will all perish. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great space: although it accommodates immeasurable worlds and beings, they all have space as their root. If space is exhausted, then the worlds and beings will all cease to exist. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great seed: although it produces immeasurable sprouts, stalks, leaves, and fruits, they all have the seed as their root. If the seed is destroyed, then the sprouts, stalks, leaves, and fruits will all wither. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, it takes the mind of awakening as its root. If the mind of awakening is cultivated, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires will naturally be extinguished. Therefore, the mind of awakening is the root of the mind of ignorance. It is also like a great river: although it flows with immeasurable currents and waves, they all have the river as their root. If the river dries up, then the currents and waves will all cease. The mind of awakening is also like this: although it gives rise to eighty-four
Furthermore, all the myriad evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have the three poisons as their root. These three poisons are greed, hatred, and delusion.
This mind of the three poisons is itself capable of encompassing all evils;
it is like a great tree whose roots, though singular, produce branches and leaves that are infinite in number. From each and every one of those roots of the three poisons, [evils] arise.
All these evil karmas, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, exceed the former by many times and are beyond comparison.

Thus, the mind of the three poisons manifests within its own essence as the six sense organs, which are also called the "six thieves"; these are the six consciousnesses. It is from these six consciousnesses that [the afflictions arise].

Moving in and out through the various sense faculties, they greedily cling to the myriad objects of the world. Capable of producing evil karma and obstructing the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are therefore called the "Six Thieves.
All sentient beings, due to these three poisons and six thieves, have their bodies and minds deluded and distracted;

they sink into birth and death, transmigrating through the six realms of existence and undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction. It is like a great river that, originating from a small spring source, flows on without ceasing until it is capable of—
It spreads and flows in waves for ten thousand *li*. Yet, if there were a person who cuts off its source, all the currents would immediately cease.
One who seeks liberation can transform the three poisons into the three groups of pure precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*), and transform the six thieves into the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
One will naturally and eternally be free from all suffering.
Question: The six destinies and the three realms are vast and boundless. If one contemplates only the mind, by what means can one escape endless suffering?
Answer: The karmic retributions of the three realms arise solely from the mind. Fundamentally, if there were no mind, one would immediately transcend the three realms.

These three realms are, in fact, the three poisons: greed constitutes the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), hatred constitutes the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and delusion constitutes the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
therefore they are called the "three realms. Due to these three poisons, one creates karma of varying weight, resulting in different retributions, and thus one is divided and assigned to them.
Because there are six bases, they are called the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).
Question: How are they divided into six according to their lightness and heaviness? Answer: Sentient beings do not understand the true cause; with deluded minds, they cultivate wholesome deeds.
One cannot avoid the three realms; thus, one is born into the three inferior destinies. What are these three inferior destinies? They are as follows:

being deluded in the practice of the ten wholesome actions while falsely seeking pleasure, one cannot avoid the realm of greed and is born into the celestial destiny. Being deluded in the observance of the five precepts while falsely giving rise to love and hatred, one cannot avoid the realm of anger and is born into the human destiny.
Being deluded in clinging to conditioned phenomena while believing in heterodox paths to seek merit, one cannot avoid the realm of ignorance and is born... [into the animal destiny].
The asura realm—these three categories are called the three light destinies. What are the three heavy destinies? They are as follows:
those who give rein to the three poisons of mind and perform only evil karma fall into the three heavy destinies. If one’s karma of greed is heavy, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts;

if one’s karma of hatred is heavy, one falls into the realm of hell; if one’s karma of delusion is heavy, one falls into the realm of animals. These two [categories of] heavy destinies are common to all.
The first three [categories of] light [karma] result in the six destinies. Thus one knows that all karma of suffering arises from the mind itself.

If one can simply collect the mind and distance oneself from all evils, the sufferings of the cycle of rebirth within the three realms and six destinies will naturally be extinguished; having left suffering behind, one immediately attains liberation.
Question: As the Buddha has taught, it was only after three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of immeasurable toil and suffering that he attained the Way of the Buddha.
Why, then, do you now say that merely observing the mind and restraining the three poisons is itself called liberation? Answer: What the Buddha has spoken contains no falsehood.
The so-called "three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas" refers precisely to the mind of the three poisons. In the language of the Hu (Central Asian), *asaṃkhyeya* means "innumerable."
The names of the kalpas in the Han language are innumerable. Within this mind of the three poisons, there are as many evil thoughts as there are sands in the Ganges River;
each and every thought constitutes one kalpa. Thus, these kalpas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and cannot be counted. Therefore, it is said that they are "three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas."

The nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is already shrouded by the three poisons. If one does not transcend those three poisons—each as numerous as the sands of three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—how can it be called liberation?

If one can now transform the minds of the three poisons, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, into the three gates of liberation, this is what is meant by attaining deliverance across the three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. [This applies to] the multitudes in the final age...
Those born with dull faculties and ignorance do not understand the Tathāgata’s teaching on the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas of secrecy;

they consequently claim that the attainment of Buddhahood will not be expected for aeons as numerous as motes of dust. Will this not mislead practitioners and cause them to retreat from the path to Bodhi?
Question: Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain the Buddha-way only by upholding the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śīkṣāpada*) and practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Now, you instruct students to merely contemplate the mind alone, without cultivating the practice of the precepts. How, then, can they become Buddhas? Answer:

The three clusters of pure precepts are precisely the restraint of the mind’s three poisons (*triviṣa*). By restraining the three poisons, one accomplishes immeasurable accumulations of goodness. An "accumulation" (*caya*) refers to a gathering.
Furthermore, immeasurable wholesome dharmas are universally gathered within the mind; therefore, it is called the Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*).

As for the six *pāramitās*, they are the purification of the six sense faculties. The foreign term is *pāramitā*; the Chinese term is "reaching the other shore. This is because the six sense faculties are purified.
To remain unstained by the six sense-objects is precisely to cross the river of afflictions and reach the shore of Bodhi; therefore, they are called the six pāramitās.
Question: As stated in the sūtras, regarding the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), there is the vow to sever all evil and the vow to cultivate all good.
[Question: You vowed to deliver all sentient beings, yet now you speak only of subduing the three poisons of the mind.
Is this not a contradiction between the words and their meaning? [Answer: What the Buddha has spoken is the word of truth.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas were practicing during past causal stages, they made three vows in response to the three poisons and maintained all pure precepts. In response to the poison of greed, they vowed: [text continues]
One cuts off all evil and constantly cultivates all that is wholesome. Facing the poison of hatred, one vows to deliver all sentient beings;

thus, one constantly cultivates wisdom. Facing the poison of delusion, by upholding these three kinds of pure dharmas—precept, concentration, and wisdom—one is able to transcend those three poisons and attain the path of Buddhahood.
The eradication of all evils is called "cutting off. By being able to uphold these three...
To gather pure precepts is to be fully endowed with all virtues; this is called cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Because one can sever evil and cultivate goodness, the myriad practices are accomplished, benefiting both oneself and others, and universally rescuing all sentient beings; therefore, it is called liberation (*vimukti*).
Thus, one should know that the cultivated practice of precepts is not separate from the mind. If one’s own mind is pure, then all Buddha-lands are entirely pure. Therefore—
The Sūtra says: "When the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; when the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure. Those who wish to attain a Buddha-field should purify their own minds.
According to the purity of the mind, so too will the Buddha-field be pure. Thus, the three clusters of pure precepts are spontaneously accomplished.
Question: As stated in the sutras, the six pāramitās are also called the six perfections—namely, giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Now, you speak of the purification of the six sense faculties as being called "pāramitās. How is this so?

If one asks how these are to be comprehensively understood, and furthermore, what is the meaning of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the answer is as follows: One who wishes to cultivate the six perfections should purify the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
First, one must subdue the six thieves. To be able to abandon the thief of the eye and remain detached from all visual objects is called generosity (*dāna*).

To be able to restrain the thief of the ear and not allow it to run wild amidst the sensory dust of sound is called ethical discipline (*śīla*). To be able to subdue the thief of the nose and treat all odors with equanimity...
Being fully endowed with self-mastery and gentle flexibility is called patience (*kṣānti*); it can subdue the thief of speech and not crave various flavors.

Praise, chanting, and exposition are called diligence (*vīrya*); it can subdue the thief of the body. Remaining serene and unmoving amidst all tactile desires is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
it can subdue the thief of the mind. Not following ignorance and constantly cultivating awakened wisdom is called wisdom (*prajñā*). These are the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
It is destiny. The six *pāramitās* are likened to a boat or raft; they can transport sentient beings to reach the other shore, and are thus called the "six perfections" (*ṣaḍ-pāramitā*).
Question: The sutra states that when Śākyamuni Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, he once drank three pecks and six sheng of milk gruel before [attaining enlightenment]. How is this so?

To attain the Way of Buddhahood, one first relies on drinking milk and subsequently realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. How could it be that liberation is attained merely through contemplating the mind?
Answer: Attaining Buddhahood is thus; these words are not false. One must indeed rely on consuming milk before one can become a Buddha.
Regarding the statement "consuming milk," there are two kinds. That which is consumed by the Buddha is not the impure milk of the mundane world, but rather that which is pure.
The "milk of the Dharma": three pecks refers to the Threefold Pure Precepts; six pints refers to the Six Pāramitās.
At the time of attaining Buddhahood, it is by consuming such pure milk of the Dharma that one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

If one were to say that the Tathāgata consumes worldly, compounded, impure, and foul-smelling cow's milk, would this not be an extreme instance of slander and delusion? True Suchness (*tathatā*) is itself gold.
The adamantine body is indestructible; the untainted *dharmakāya* is forever free from all worldly sufferings.
Why, then, should it require such impure milk to satisfy its hunger and thirst? As the Sūtra says: "That cow does not dwell on high plateaus, nor does it dwell in low-lying marshes."
It does not eat grain, wheat, chaff, or bran; it does not herd with female cows. That cow’s body is the color of purple-polished gold.

As for the "cow," it refers to Vairocana Buddha. Out of great compassion and pity for all beings, he produces from within the pure essence of the Dharma such subtle and wondrous milk of the Dharma—the three clusters of pure precepts and the six *pāramitās*—to nourish [beings].
It nurtures all who seek liberation. Such is the truly pure cow and its pure milk;
not only does the Tathāgata drink it to achieve the Way, but if any sentient beings can drink it, they shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Question: The sutras state that the Buddha commanded sentient beings to construct monasteries, cast and carve images, burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, circumambulate stupas and practice walking meditation throughout the six periods of day and night, observe the fasts, and perform prostrations—claiming that through these various merits, one attains the Way of the Buddha.
If one were to claim that merely contemplating the mind subsumes all such practices, then speaking in this way would be as empty as space. Answer:
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha contain immeasurable skillful means because all sentient beings possess dull faculties and narrow capacities, and thus do not realize the profoundly deep meaning.

For this reason, he provisionally uses conditioned phenomena as metaphors for the unconditioned. If one does not cultivate internal practice but merely seeks externally, hoping thereby to obtain merit, such a thing is impossible.
As for the term "gārala," it is a word from the two [ancient] kingdoms; in the language of India, it refers to this land.

This is translated as the "Pure Land. If one eternally eliminates the three poisons, constantly purifies the six sense faculties, and remains serene in body and mind such that both internal and external are pure, this is called cultivating a *saṃghārāma*.
As for those who cast and fashion images, they are all sentient beings seeking the Buddha-way.
Since they perform various practices of awakening to emulate the true countenance and wondrous marks of the Tathāgata, how could they be dismissed?
This is the casting of [the Buddha] in gold and copper. Therefore, those who seek liberation take the body as the furnace, the Dharma as the fire, and wisdom as the skilled artisan.

Taking the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) as the mold, they smelt and refine the *tathatā* buddha-nature within the body, causing it to enter entirely into the molds of all the precepts. Thus, with reverence, one should practice and uphold them. One.
It is without leakage or deficiency; it naturally accomplishes the image of the true countenance.
This is what is called the ultimately eternal and subtle form-body (*rūpakāya*), which is not a conditioned phenomenon subject to decay.

If a person seeks the Way yet does not understand how to cast and write this true countenance in this manner, on what basis could they rashly speak of its merit? As for the burning of incense, it is likewise not the incense of worldly forms; rather, it is...
This is the fragrance of the unconditioned True Dharma. It permeates all foul odors—the ignorance and evil karma—and causes them all to be extinguished.
This fragrance of the True Dharma is of five kinds: first is the fragrance of morality (*śīla*), which means being able to sever all evils and cultivate all virtues;
second is the fragrance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which means having deep faith in the Mahāyāna with a mind that never regresses; third is the fragrance of wisdom (*prajñā*).
That which is called constantly observing within one’s own body and mind: the fourth is the fragrance of liberation, which means being able to sever all fetters of ignorance;
the fifth is the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation, which means that contemplation is ever-luminous and penetrates all things without obstruction.
These five kinds of fragrance are called the supreme fragrances, peerless in the world. When the Buddha was in the world...
[The Buddha] commanded his disciples to use the fire of wisdom to burn such priceless, precious incense as an offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At present, sentient beings do not understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata;

they merely take external fire to burn worldly, obstructive incenses such as aloeswood (*agaru*), sandalwood (*candana*), and frankincense (*turuṣka*), hoping thereby for karmic rewards. How could they obtain them? As for "scattering flowers," this is the meaning.
It is also thus. That which is called "Kai" (豈) refers to the preaching of the True Dharma.
These flowers of merit benefit sentient beings, scattering and moistening all things, universally bestowing adornment upon the nature of *tathatā*. These flowers of merit are praised by the Buddhas;

they abide eternally and ultimately, with no time of fading or falling away. If there should be a person who scatters such flowers, they shall obtain immeasurable merit. If one says "like... [the analogy follows].
To come and command sentient beings to cut and trim silken fabrics or harm and damage plants and trees in order to scatter them as flowers—such a thing is impossible.
Why is this? One who upholds the pure precepts does not allow any violation against the myriad phenomena of the heavens, the earth, and all that exists within them.
If one incurs a grave offense even through an accidental transgression, how much more so now when one intentionally destroys the pure precepts?

To harm all living beings while seeking a reward of merit—to desire benefit yet instead incur loss—is this even possible? Furthermore, the long-burning lamp is none other than the mind of perfect enlightenment.
Because clear awareness is like a lamp, all those seeking liberation take the body as the lamp-stand and the mind as the wick;
they increase their various virtuous conducts as the addition of oil, and their penetrating wisdom is likened to the light of the flame.
One should constantly burn such a lamp of true awakening to shatter all the darkness of ignorance and delusion. By means of this...

The Dharma is thus transmitted and revealed to one another; it is like a single lamp that kindles hundreds of thousands of lamps, continuing the illumination so that the lighting of lamps is inexhaustible, and is therefore called "Ever-Bright.
There was a Buddha in the past named Dīpaṃkara (The Lamp-Lighter); the meaning is likewise the same.
Foolish sentient beings do not understand the Tathāgata’s skillful teaching; they practice only in delusion and cling to conditioned phenomena, and thus they light the worldly [fires].
To light a lamp of ghee and oil to illuminate an empty room and claim this conforms to the teachings—is this not erroneous? Why is this so?
When the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from the *ūrṇā-kośa* between his eyebrows, it was able to illuminate eighteen thousand worlds above;

how could such a benefit as that be achieved by a lamp of ghee and oil? Upon careful examination of this principle, one must conclude that it is not so. Furthermore, regarding the six periods of the day...

Regarding "practicing the Way": this refers to constantly practicing the Buddha-way at all times within the six sense faculties, cultivating various practices of awakening, and subduing the six faculties without abandoning them for a long duration;
these are called the "six periods. Regarding "circumambulating the stupa while practicing the Way": the stupa is the body and mind.
One should cause the wisdom of awakening to circumambulate the body and mind, with every thought-moment proceeding without ceasing; this is called "circumambulating the stupa. To transcend—
All past sages practiced this path and thereby attained nirvana. Yet nowadays, people of the world do not comprehend this principle;

they never practice internally, but only cling to external seeking. They take their physical bodies, which are composed of obstructive matter, and circumambulate stupas throughout the world, rushing about day and night.
This merely exhausts them in vain, providing no benefit whatsoever to true nature. Furthermore, those who observe the fast must understand its underlying meaning.
"Dasi-li" (達斯理) is merely a transliteration. "Zhai" (齋) means "to align" (*qi*). What is called *zhai* is to align and rectify the body and mind, not allowing them to become distracted.
"Chi" (持) means "to protect. What is called *chi* is to protect and maintain all precepts and practices according to the Dharma.

One must externally restrain the six sense-faculties and internally control the three poisons; diligently practicing introspection to purify the body and mind—understanding this meaning is what is called observing the fast (*zhichai*). Furthermore,
For those who observe the fast, there are five kinds of sustenance: first, the food of Dharma-joy, which refers to relying upon and upholding the True Dharma while joyfully practicing it;
second, the food of meditative rapture, which refers to inner and outer tranquility and the resulting delight of body and mind;

third, the food of mindfulness, which refers to constantly recollecting all Buddhas with the harmony of mind and speech; fourth, the food of aspiration, which refers to [the practice of] walking, standing, and sitting...
While lying down, one should always seek virtuous aspirations. Fifth is the food of liberation, which means that the mind is constantly pure and unstained by worldly dust.
These five kinds of food are called the food of the fast. Furthermore, if there is anyone who does not eat these five kinds of pure food, [they do not partake in the fast].

To claim that one maintains the fast [by merely abstaining from food] is impossible. Only by severing the food of ignorance does one truly maintain it; if one happens to touch it, it is called breaking the fast.
If the fast is broken, how can one obtain merit? There are deluded people in the world who do not realize this principle;

their bodies and minds are dissolute, and they commit all manner of evils because they indulge their passions out of greed, feeling no shame or remorse, yet believing that they can achieve it for themselves simply by cutting off external food.
Regarding the observance of the fast (*upavāsa*), such a thing certainly does not exist [in the ultimate sense]. Furthermore, as for prostration (*vandanā*), it should follow this method:

one must have internal clarity through principle (*li*) while affairs (*shi*) adapt to provisional transformations. When principle possesses both manifestation and concealment, and one realizes this meaning, it is called "relying on the Dharma.
Now, ritual (*li*) is reverence; prostration (*bai*) is submission. What is meant by "reverently honoring the true nature" and "submitting to and subduing ignorance" is what is termed "prostration."
If one can forever extinguish unwholesome states and maintain wholesome thoughts at all times, even though no outward form is manifest, this is called prostration.

Its characteristic is precisely the characteristic of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). The World-Honored One, wishing to cause worldly people to express a humble and submissive mind, also prescribes prostration;

therefore, one must bend the outer body to demonstrate inner reverence. By manifesting the external, the internal is clarified; thus nature and characteristics correspond. If one does not practice this further...
Regarding the principle of the Dharma: if one clings solely to seeking it externally while neglecting the internal, then one will give rein to anger and ignorance, constantly committing evil deeds.

Externally, this is merely a vain exertion of physical form, feigning dignified deportment; such a person has no sense of shame before the sages and only deceives the common folk. They cannot escape saṃsāra, so how could they ever achieve spiritual merit?
Question: As stated in the *Jentāka-sūtra*, bathing the Sangha yields immeasurable merit.
This appears to rely upon ritual acts (*vastu-dharma*), through which merit is first accomplished. Would this be compatible with the practice of contemplating the mind? Answer:
Bathing the Sangha does not refer to washing mundane, conditioned things. The World-Honored One once preached the *Jentāka-sūtra* for his disciples with the intention that—
In order to uphold the ritual of bathing, worldly affairs are employed as metaphors for the True Teaching.
Thus, the merit of the seven items of offering is explained through concealed discourse. What are these seven items? First, pure water; second, burning fire;
third, cleansing powder; fourth, willow twigs; fifth, pure ash; sixth, clarified butter; and seventh, undergarments. These seven dharmas serve as metaphors.
Regarding these seven matters: by means of these seven dharmas, all sentient beings bathe and adorn themselves, able to eliminate the poisonous mind and the defilements of ignorance.
As for these seven dharmas: the first is pure precepts, which wash away transgressions and improprieties, just as pure water cleanses all dust and grime.
The second is wisdom, which observes both the internal and external, just as lighting a fire can warm pure water.
Third is discernment (*viveka*), which rejects all evils, just as cleansing soap can purify grime and oil.

Fourth is reality (*tattva*), which severs all deluded thoughts, just as chewing a *dantakāṣṭha* twig can purify the breath. Fifth is right faith (*samyak-prasāda*), which is resolute and free from doubt.
First is like rubbing the body with pure ash, which can ward off all winds. Second is gentleness and patience, which is like clarified butter (*sarpis*) that permeates and moistens the skin.
Third is shame and remorse, which repent for all evil deeds; it is like an undergarment that conceals an unseemly form.
These seven dharmas mentioned above are the secret meanings within this sutra. The Tathāgata shall thus [explain them] for the sake of the great [disciples].
This was spoken for those of sharp faculties, not for ordinary persons of small wisdom and inferior capacity; therefore, people of today are unable to understand or realize it.
As for the "warm bathhouse," this refers to the body itself. Thus, one kindles the fire of wisdom and warms the waters of pure precepts to bathe the True Suchness and Buddha-nature within the body.
One should uphold the seven dharmas to adorn oneself. At that time, the bhikṣu was wise...
Those of superior intelligence clearly understand the intent of the Sages; practicing according to the teachings, they achieve merit and together ascend to the fruits of sainthood.
The sentient beings of the present age cannot fathom these matters; using worldly water to wash their obstructed physical bodies, they claim to rely upon the sutras—is this not an error?
Furthermore, True Suchness and Buddha-nature are not of an ordinary form, and the defilements of affliction are originally without characteristics.
How could one possibly use obstructive water to wash an unconditioned body? Such a practice is inconsistent with reality; how, then, could it lead to the realization of the Way?
If you wish for the body to attain purity, you should contemplate this body as having originally arisen from the impurity of craving and desire, filled with stench and filth.
It is filled both internally and externally. If one seeks purity by washing this body, it is like a moat that can only be cleansed once it has been completely drained.
Judging by this, it is clear that washing the exterior is not the teaching of the Buddha.
Question: The sutras state that by recollecting the Buddha with a sincere mind, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land.

Since this single gateway should lead directly to Buddhahood, why rely on contemplating the mind to seek liberation? Answer: Now, one who recollects the Buddha must maintain right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

That which is definitive in meaning (*nītārtha*) is right; that which is not definitive in meaning (*neyārtha*) is wrong. Through right mindfulness, one will certainly attain rebirth; as for wrong mindfulness, how could it possibly succeed?
To reach that state: "Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*). This refers to being vigilant regarding body and mind so as not to allow evil to arise.
"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) means recollection; it refers to maintaining the observance of precepts without forgetfulness and applying oneself with diligent clarity.

Such meanings are termed "mindfulness. Therefore, one should know that mindfulness resides in the mind and not in words. One uses the trap to seek the fish; once the fish is caught, one forgets the trap. One uses words to seek the meaning.
When one attains the meaning, one forgets the words. Since you have invoked the name of the Buddha through recitation, you must understand the Way of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*).

If the mind lacks sincerity while the mouth utters empty names, the three poisons will surge within and the conceit of self and others will fill the breast; thus, with an ignorant mind, one will fail to see the Buddha and labor in vain.
Furthermore, there is a vast difference in meaning between "reciting" and "recollecting. To speak it with the mouth is called "reciting"; to contemplate it with the mind is called...
Reflecting on this, one knows that mindfulness arises from the mind; it is called the gateway of awakening practice. To recite [the words] within the mouth is merely the characteristic of sound.
To grasp at characteristics in search of the principle is ultimately impossible. Therefore, one knows that what was cultivated by all the sages of the past was not external teaching;
it was simply a matter of investigating the mind. Thus, the mind itself is the source of all virtues, and the mind itself is the foundation of the myriad qualities.
"Lord, the Nirvana of eternal bliss arises from the stilling of the mind; the saṃsāra of the three realms likewise originates from the mind.
The mind is the gateway to this world, and the mind is the passageway to liberation. If one knows the gateway of the mind, why worry about the difficulty of accomplishment?

If one knows the passageway, why fear not reaching the goal? I observe that those of shallow understanding nowadays know only to take ritual appearances as their merit. [The text continues: "Extensively..."

They squander wealth and treasures, causing great harm to both land and water creatures. They vainly construct images and stupas, pointlessly pressuring laborers. Piling up wood and layering mud, they apply blue pigments and paint borders;
they exhaust their hearts and strength, harming themselves while deluding others. Lacking any sense of shame or remorse, how could they ever awaken from this mire?
Seeing conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), they are zealously attached to them; when hearing of signlessness (*animitta*), they remain dazed as if lost. Furthermore, they crave the present world...

O Little Compassion, how can you fail to perceive the great suffering of the future? This cultivation of study is merely a waste of effort; it turns one’s back on the Right Path and returns one to the heterodox, deceiving oneself with claims of attaining merit.
Rather, one should simply be able to gather the mind for inward illumination and maintain clear observation of the external world.

By severing the three poisons so they are forever extinguished, and by warding off the six thieves so they cannot cause further disturbance, the infinite merits of the Ganges-sand will naturally manifest in all manner of adornments.
The various dharma-gates are each fully accomplished; transcending the mundane, one realizes the holy. To witness this face-to-face is not remote; awakening occurs in an instant.

Why trouble oneself until one’s hair turns white? The true gate is profound and secret; how could it be fully set forth? I shall briefly describe the contemplation of the mind, detailing but a small portion thereof, and thus speak in verse:
Originally I sought the mind, yet the mind itself was what held me; seeking the mind, I could not find it, so I waited for the mind to know itself.
Buddhahood is not found outside of the mind; when the mind arises, it is precisely at that moment that transgression arises.
Originally I sought the mind and did not seek the Buddha, for I clearly realized that the three realms are empty and devoid of substance.
If you wish to seek the Buddha, seek only the mind; this very mind, mind after mind, is the Buddha.
— From the *Poxiang Lun* (Treatise on the Shattering of Characteristics) by Master Bodhidharma.
